newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran presidential campaign shifts into top gear.
newsitem.headline: Iran presidential campaign shifts into top gear.

text.p: Iranians drove across the capital Tehran on Tuesady in cars plastered with large posters of their favourite presidential candidates as the race for the May 23 election gained pace.

Residents said walls, storefronts and even traffic signs were covered with campaign material despite rules allowing posters and banners only outside campaign offices of the four men seeking to replace President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.
Some shopkeepers handed out election leaflets to customers while rival groups tore down each others' posters or covered them with their own, they said.

Yellow banners supporting conservative parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri and blue ones put up by pro-Rafsanjani supporters of former culture minister Mohammad Khatami both called for wide popular participation in the polls.
State radio and television repeatedly carried a call by supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei urging clerics to help voters choose the candidate with the best Islamic credentials.
Analysts said the call was likely to help Nateq-Nouri, who is close to Iran's traditional bazaar merchants and has received the backing of important clergy groups.

The Guardian Council, a powerful Islamic screening body that approved the four candidates and rejected 234 others who signed up to run, said it had voted Nateq-Nouri as the most highly qualified of the four, state-run Tehran radio said.

The announcement was likely to boost Nateq-Nouri's chances by prompting mainstream clerics to launch a campaign in his support during major annual Shi'ite mourning ceremonies on Friday and Saturday, the analysts said.

Khatami, a Shi'ite clergyman like Nateq-Nouri, is seen as a being a tolerant politician and draws support from a coalition of pro-Rafsanjani centrists and Islamist left-wingers who have moderated many of their views in recent years.

Tehran residents said Khatami had gained wide support among women, young people and intellectuals who fear a harder application of Islamic rules in everyday life and restrictions on freedom of expression if Nateq-Nouri was elected.
The other candidates are hardline conservative Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri, a former intelligence minister, and Reza Zavarei, a conservative who is deputy head of the judiciary.
The four were approved after being screened for their allegiance to Iran's Islamic government system and "absolute obedience" to Khamenei.
Some 33 million Iranians aged 15 years and older are eligible to vote in the polls, Iran's seventh presidential election since the 1979 revolution.

Rafsanjani must stand down in August after two four-year terms but is expected to continue to wield considerable influence in state affairs as head of a powerful body that will draw up government policies and advise Khamenei.
